Shai-Hulud npm worm payload/workflow file drop (bundle.js, setup_bun.js, shai-hulud-workflow.yml) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud supply-chain worm dropping its self-replicating payload and CI persistence file onto developer machines during npm install. Fires on the confirmed malicious bundle.js SHA256 or the distinctive worm filenames written by node/npm. Rationale: Uses the second-source-confirmed Shai-Hulud bundle.js SHA256 (46faab8a...) and the campaign's distinctive filenames (shai-hulud-workflow.yml, setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) named across Unit42/Wiz/Datadog write-ups of the article's flagship campaign; hash+filename anchors make this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately named a file bundle.js under a non-malicious .github/workflows path (rare — that dir holds YAML, not JS)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a Shai-Hulud sample in a sandbox/analysis VM
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies of the payload re-triggering the file-write event from the quarantine folder
  • Threat-intel/IR team staging IOC files named setup_bun.js for tabletop or purple-team exercises
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Windows Defender\", @"\Quarantine\") or DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName node.exe/npm) and the folder — a real hit is bundle.js/setup_bun.js executed during an npm/bun install in a repo working dir. Check the file SHA256 against 46faab8a... 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, revoke and rotate all npm tokens, GitHub PATs, and cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure) keys used from it; check GitHub for a newly-created public repo named 'Shai-Hulud' and any 'shai-hulud-workflow.yml' pushed to your repos. 3) HUNT: Pivot to outbound connections to webhook.site from the same host, enumerate every package version installed in the last 24h, and scope other developers who installed the same dependency.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (SHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09")
     or FileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
     or (FileName =~ "bundle.js" and FolderPath has @"\.github\workflows")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileSHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09")
     or TargetFileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
     or (TargetFileName =~ "bundle.js" and TargetFilePath has @"\.github\workflows")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud credential exfiltration: node/npm outbound to webhook.site AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud worm's credential exfiltration stage where the postinstall payload beacons harvested npm/GitHub/cloud tokens to the hardcoded webhook.site drop (bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7). Pairs the webhook.site destination with a node/npm/bun/git initiating process to cut the FP from legit webhook testing. Rationale: Anchors on the second-source-confirmed hardcoded exfil host webhook.site (Shai-Hulud endpoint bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) but requires a node/npm/bun/git initiating process so it fires on postinstall exfil, not a developer manually testing a webhook in a browser. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1567 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using webhook.site to test an outbound webhook from a Node app during development
  • CI runner (node/git) hitting a webhook.site URL configured in a test suite or integration fixture
  • QA automation posting to webhook.site as a capture endpoint
  • Internal tooling that uses webhook.site free-tier bins for prototyping event delivery
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","postinstall","ci","exec") and not (DeviceName has_any ("build-agent","ci-runner") and InitiatingProcessAccountName has "jenkins")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full RemoteUrl/DNS path — a real hit posts to a webhook.site UUID bin (campaign default bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) shortly after an npm/bun install; check InitiatingProcessCommandLine for a package install and correlate with a bundle.js/setup_bun.js write in the last hour. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, immediately rotate npm tokens, GitHub PATs, and AWS/GCP/Azure keys from that machine, and block webhook.site at egress. 3) HUNT: Search GitHub audit for a new public 'Shai-Hulud' repo or 'shai-hulud-workflow.yml' commits under affected users, and scope every other host that installed the same package version.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "webhook.site"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","bun.exe","git.exe","curl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "webhook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Shai-Hulud Credential Exfiltration to webhook.site via node/npm
id: 2b9e4d17-5c60-49af-8f31-a0d6c2e51f4a
description: Detects Node/npm/bun/git process resolving or connecting to webhook.site, the Shai-Hulud worm's hardcoded token exfiltration endpoint
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/aikido-intel-detects-malware-vulnerabilities-first
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
  - https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1567
  - attack.t1552.001
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '\git.exe'
    DestinationHostname|contains: 'webhook.site'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:webhook.site @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\npm.exe OR *\bun.exe OR *\git.exe)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/webhook\.site$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|bun|git)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="webhook.site" OR DNS.query="*.webhook.site") by DNS.src DNS.dest DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="webhook.site" OR DNS.query="*.webhook.site") by DNS.src DNS.dest DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or SHA1 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or SHA1 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] First-seen Salesforce Connected App performing bulk API / report export (fake Data Loader) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Salesforce Connected App API activity from ShinyHunters integration-abuse IPs · [LLM] Anomalous Salesforce ReportExport volume — bulk CRM exfiltration · [LLM] Guest-user Aura/GraphQL mass data retrieval from ShinyHunters IOC IP · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Salesforce Connected App API activity from ShinyHunters integration-abuse IPs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts Salesforce API/CRM query activity attributed to a Connected App originating from the specific source IPs Microsoft tied to ShinyHunters/UNC6395 abuse of trusted OAuth integrations (Salesloft Drift, Gainsight, Klue). Because the actors ride sanctioned OAuth tokens, IP is the highest-fidelity anchor available on this telemetry. Rationale: Anchors on the five Microsoft-published IOC IPs (article Table 2; 138.226.246.94 is explicitly the Klue integration performing CRM API queries) scoped to Salesforce API/Connected-App activity — a fixed IP set on SaaS API telemetry is an alerting-grade match with near-zero legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html
ATT&CKT1199 T1550.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate integration vendor (Klue/Gainsight) re-uses one of these IPs post-remediation for sanctioned traffic
  • Corporate egress NAT coincidentally shares an IP block with a listed address
  • Threat-intel enrichment jobs or a SOC replay hitting the Salesforce API from a sinkholed IP
  • Security researcher / IR team validating the IOC against the tenant
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all CloudAppEvents for the matched IP, note the ConnectedAppId and AccountDisplayName acting on its behalf, and confirm whether the app is an approved Salesloft/Gainsight/Klue integration. 2) Contain: in Salesforce, revoke the Connected App's OAuth tokens and block the source IP at the org login-IP-range/Connected-App policy; rotate the integration's connection secret. 3) Hunt: enumerate every ReportExport/BulkApi call by that ConnectedAppId, pivot to other tenants/users the same app touched, and search for the remaining four IOC IPs and any credentials exposed in exported records.
let IocIps = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where IPAddress in (IocIps)
| extend ConnectedAppId = tostring(coalesce(RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID, RawEventData.ConnectedAppId))
| summarize Events=count(), Actions=make_set(ActionType,10), ConnectedApps=make_set(ConnectedAppId,10), Users=make_set(AccountDisplayName,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode
| order by Events desc

First-seen Salesforce Connected App performing bulk API / report export (fake Data Loader) AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces a Connected App ID that has never been observed in the tenant baseline suddenly issuing API calls or report exports — the pattern left by ShinyHunters' vishing-driven OAuth consent to a malicious app disguised as the legitimate Salesforce Data Loader. Catches consent-phishing even when the source IP is not a known IOC. Rationale: Uses the article's own ConnectedAppId extraction (RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID / ConnectedAppId, code Block 1) but replaces the non-schema UncommonForUser flag with a 30-day first-seen anti-join — a newly-consented app doing bulk API/export is exactly the malicious 'Data Loader' behaviour Microsoft describes. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new integration onboarded by IT during the lookback window (e.g. a sanctioned analytics or backup app)
  • Salesforce Data Loader genuinely used by an admin for a one-off migration
  • Connected App re-registered with a new ID after a secret rotation
  • Sandbox-to-prod app promotion generating a first-seen ID
Suppression filter
| where UAs has_any ("python","Salesforce-","Bulk API","axios","node-fetch","Go-http-client") or Events > 500  // narrow to automated bulk-access user-agents / high volume
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ConnectedApp's granted OAuth scopes and the consenting user; check whether the consent event correlates with a help-desk/vishing report or an unusual admin session. 2) Contain: revoke the app's tokens, remove the Connected App, and force-reauth/reset the consenting user if a scope like api or full was granted. 3) Hunt: list every record type queried/exported by the app, cross-reference the five IOC IPs, and review other users who consented to the same app name across the tenant.

Anomalous Salesforce ReportExport volume — bulk CRM exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a Salesforce user identity exporting reports at a volume far above normal, the mass-exfiltration step Microsoft observed across all three ShinyHunters intrusion paths (accounts, contacts, and service-case data pulled at scale). Pivots on Salesforce report-export events rather than authentication, which the actors evade. Rationale: Built directly on the article's ReportExport code (Block 2, RawEventData.USER_ID) and Microsoft's 'Possible Salesforce scraping activity' coverage; a per-hour export burst is the concrete exfiltration signal for accounts/contacts/case data the actors bulk-queried. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://www.mitiga.io/blog/shinyhunters-and-unc6395-inside-the-salesforce-and-salesloft-breaches
ATT&CKT1567 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Quarterly business-review or finance close where an analyst legitimately exports many reports
  • A scheduled BI/ETL service account performing routine bulk report pulls
  • Data-migration or Salesforce backup job running as a user identity
  • Sales-ops power user building a large territory dataset
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName has_any ("svc","integration","backup","etl") and UAs has_any ("Salesforce Reporting","DataLoader","Informatica"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the SalesforceUserId is a human, an integration/service account, or a hijacked session; compare the export IPs/user-agents against the five IOC IPs and the user's normal geo. 2) Contain: suspend the Salesforce session/user and revoke associated OAuth grants; enable/verify Salesforce Shield Event Monitoring transaction security to block further exports. 3) Hunt: enumerate the specific reports/objects exported, assess data sensitivity, and pivot to Connected-App attribution to see if the exports rode a compromised integration token.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType == "ReportExport"
| extend SalesforceUserId = tostring(RawEventData.USER_ID)
| summarize Exports=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), UAs=make_set(UserAgent,10) by bin(Timestamp, 1h), AccountObjectId, AccountId, AccountDisplayName, SalesforceUserId
| where Exports > 50   // 50 exports/hr >> typical per-user report cadence; empirical bulk-exfil threshold
| order by Exports desc

Guest-user Aura/GraphQL mass data retrieval from ShinyHunters IOC IP AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts unauthenticated guest-user Salesforce activity from IOC IP 103.75.11.78 (Microsoft: targeting the Aura framework via guest access, 19–22 June), where chained Aura/GraphQL requests circumvented record-retrieval limits to scrape data far beyond normal guest scope. Targets the misconfigured-guest-access intrusion path. Rationale: Anchors on the single IOC IP Microsoft attributes specifically to Aura-framework guest-access data theft (Table 2, 19–22 June window) and surfaces the guest/USER_TYPE context — a fixed IP tied to a named intrusion path makes this alerting-grade and distinct from the integration-IP UC. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift
ATT&CKT1213 T1078.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A vulnerability scanner or bug-bounty researcher probing the org's Experience Cloud / Aura endpoints from that IP after IOC publication
  • Legitimate high-volume anonymous community-portal browsing sharing the IP via CGNAT
  • IR/pentest engagement replaying the Aura request chain for validation
  • Third-party uptime monitor hitting public community pages
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the activity is guest/unauthenticated (USER_TYPE) and enumerate the Aura/GraphQL endpoints and objects returned; determine which guest-exposed records were reachable. 2) Contain: tighten guest-user object/field permissions and sharing rules on the affected Experience Cloud site, disable unauthenticated Aura endpoints not required, and block the IP. 3) Hunt: review all guest-user activity across community sites for chained Aura/GraphQL scraping patterns and abnormally large result sets, and check for the same IP against the other Salesforce intrusion paths.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

DeviceProcessEvents

SecurityEvent

status: experimental

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

CloudAppEvents

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] DIRAC FileCatalog/Tornado service spawns shell or recon binary (CVE-2026-61667 eval RCE)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DIRAC dirac.cfg secrets read via shell utility (post-RCE credential access) · [LLM] DIRAC log evidence removal under /opt/dirac (post-RCE anti-forensics)
DIRAC FileCatalog/Tornado service spawns shell or recon binary (CVE-2026-61667 eval RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE landing for CVE-2026-61667: the DIRAC FileCatalog DatasetManager passes SQL-injection-controlled data into eval(), so the DIRAC service Python process (Tornado/dirac-service under /opt/dirac) executing an attacker payload will spawn a shell or recon/download binary. A DIRAC data service should never fork /bin/sh, id, whoami, curl or nc, making the parent→child pair high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchors on the DIRAC service invocation strings (tornado-start-all, DataManagement/FileCatalog, TornadoFileCatalogHandler, dirac-service) and /opt/dirac runtime path confirmed in DIRAC docs, paired with a shell/recon child set — the exact behaviour of an eval() RCE landing. Cross-checked GHSA + GitLab advisory mirror; DIRAC HTTPS/Tornado service docs confirm the handler path and /opt/dirac supervision. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/ • https://dirac.readthedocs.io/en/latest/AdministratorGuide/ServerInstallations/HTTPSServices.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC agent/service legitimately shelling out to curl/wget to fetch CA CRLs or CVMFS content
  • Admin-invoked health-check or monitoring plugin running under the dirac service tree
  • Backup or housekeeping cron launched from the DIRAC runit environment calling sh/bash
  • DIRAC pilot/job wrappers invoking id/hostname during environment setup
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("crl","cvmfs","/ca/","cern.ch"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full process tree for the flagged child — confirm the parent is the FileCatalog/Tornado Python process and inspect the child command line for reverse-shell, download, or recon intent; correlate with FileCatalog service access logs for a preceding checkDataset call. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and rotate everything the DIRAC service can reach — dirac.cfg DB credentials, all stored proxies and tokens — since RCE implies full secret exposure. Step 3 (hunt): Search the same host and peer DIRAC servers for reads of dirac.cfg, proxy/token exfiltration, and log tampering (UCs 2 and 3); verify DIRAC is patched to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/opt/dirac/"
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("tornado-start-all","DataManagement/FileCatalog","dirac-service","TornadoFileCatalogHandler")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "/")[-1])
| where ActingProcessName startswith "/opt/dirac/"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("tornado-start-all","DataManagement/FileCatalog","dirac-service","TornadoFileCatalogHandler")
| where ChildName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ChildName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DIRAC FileCatalog Service Spawns Shell or Recon Binary
id: 6f2a1d4e-9c3b-4a1e-8f7d-2b5c0e1a7d33
description: Detects the DIRAC FileCatalog/Tornado service process (under /opt/dirac) spawning a shell or recon/download binary, consistent with CVE-2026-61667 eval-based RCE.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|startswith: '/opt/dirac/'
  parent_cmd:
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'tornado-start-all'
      - 'DataManagement/FileCatalog'
      - 'dirac-service'
      - 'TornadoFileCatalogHandler'
  child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/id'
      - '/whoami'
      - '/uname'
      - '/hostname'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/perl'
  condition: (parent or parent_cmd) and child
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @user.name:dirac @process.name:(sh OR bash OR dash OR zsh OR id OR whoami OR uname OR hostname OR curl OR wget OR nc OR ncat OR perl)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentImageFileName=/\/opt\/dirac\//i OR ParentBaseFileName=/(tornado|dirac)/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|id|whoami|uname|hostname|curl|wget|nc|ncat|perl)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.process_path) as process_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_path="/opt/dirac/*" OR Processes.parent_process="*tornado-start-all*" OR Processes.parent_process="*DataManagement/FileCatalog*" OR Processes.parent_process="*dirac-service*" OR Processes.parent_process="*TornadoFileCatalogHandler*") (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.process_path) as process_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_path="/opt/dirac/*" OR Processes.parent_process="*tornado-start-all*" OR Processes.parent_process="*DataManagement/FileCatalog*" OR Processes.parent_process="*dirac-service*" OR Processes.parent_process="*TornadoFileCatalogHandler*") (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
DIRAC dirac.cfg secrets read via shell utility (post-RCE credential access) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-harvesting step called out in CVE-2026-61667: after RCE the attacker reads /opt/dirac/etc/dirac.cfg to obtain database passwords. Legitimately dirac.cfg is only parsed by the DIRAC Python runtime, so a cat/grep/less/strings process whose command line references dirac.cfg is a strong indicator of manual secret theft. Rationale: dirac.cfg is named in the advisory as the file holding DB passwords; it is normally read only by the DIRAC Python runtime, so an interactive reader binary referencing it is a precise credential-theft signal with minimal legitimate use. Second-sourced via the GitLab advisory mirror. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC administrator manually inspecting or grepping dirac.cfg during troubleshooting
  • Config-management/backup tooling (cp/scp) copying dirac.cfg as part of host provisioning
  • Ops runbook using strings/cat to diff configuration between DIRAC nodes
  • Site packaging scripts templating dirac.cfg with sed
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet","salt-minion","cfengine") or FileName in~ ("cp","scp") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cron","crond"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating user and parent process — if the reader was spawned from the FileCatalog/Tornado service tree (UC1) rather than an interactive admin session, treat as confirmed theft. Step 2 (contain): Immediately rotate every credential in dirac.cfg (database passwords, connection secrets) and force re-issuance of any proxies/tokens managed by this instance; isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same host for outbound transfer of the config (scp/curl uploads), proxy/token DB dumps, and evidence removal (UC3); check whether the same account read dirac.cfg on other DIRAC servers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "dirac.cfg"
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","egrep","zgrep","less","more","head","tail","awk","sed","strings","xxd","od","vi","vim","nano","cp","scp","base64")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "/")[-1])
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "dirac.cfg"
| where ChildName in~ ("cat","grep","egrep","zgrep","less","more","head","tail","awk","sed","strings","xxd","od","vi","vim","nano","cp","scp","base64")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ChildName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DIRAC log evidence removal under /opt/dirac (post-RCE anti-forensics) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the log-tampering step the advisory notes an attacker can perform after RCE ('remove evidence of the exploit from the log'). Detects rm/shred/truncate/unlink/sed targeting files under the DIRAC install tree's log directories, excluding the legitimate svlogd/logrotate rotation processes. Rationale: Uses the advisory's explicit note that an attacker can remove exploit evidence from local logs, anchored to the /opt/dirac install tree confirmed in DIRAC docs and scoped to destructive utilities while excluding the svlogd/logrotate rotation that legitimately manages DIRAC logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/ • https://dirac.readthedocs.io/en/latest/AdministratorGuide/ServerInstallations/HTTPSServices.html
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1070.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually clearing stuck/oversized DIRAC service logs during maintenance
  • Custom cleanup cron pruning old /opt/dirac/runit log directories
  • DIRAC upgrade/reinstall scripts removing prior version log trees
  • Disk-space remediation runbooks truncating verbose component logs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("logrotate","svlogd","dirac-install","install_site")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine what was deleted/truncated and by which user and parent process; if the deleting process descends from the FileCatalog/Tornado service tree or a shell spawned by it (UC1), treat as anti-forensics. Step 2 (contain): Preserve remaining logs and disk artifacts (snapshot the volume), isolate the host, and pull any centrally-forwarded copies of the destroyed DIRAC logs before they age out. Step 3 (hunt): Reconstruct the timeline from surviving central logs — look for the preceding FileCatalog checkDataset request, shell spawn (UC1), and dirac.cfg/secret access (UC2) on this and peer DIRAC nodes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("rm","shred","truncate","unlink","sed")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/opt/dirac/" and ProcessCommandLine has "log"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svlogd","logrotate")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "/")[-1]), ParentName = tostring(split(ActingProcessName, "/")[-1])
| where ChildName in~ ("rm","shred","truncate","unlink","sed")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "/opt/dirac/" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "log"
| where ParentName !in~ ("svlogd","logrotate")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ChildName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-07-13 9 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a new macOS information stealer called CrashStealer that's capable of harvesting sensitive data from compromised systems. Unlike other information stealers that are built on AppleScript droppers or Objective-C-based wrappers, CrashStealer is implemented in native C++, according to Jamf Threat Labs. CrashStealer 'veltod' dropper execution from mounted Werkbit.app DMG AIDelivery High
Hunts execution of the notarized CrashStealer first-stage binary 'veltod' (bundle dev.golove.velto) launched from a mounted Werkbit.app disk image. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact malicious executable name and the /Volumes-mounted Werkbit.app container that clears Gatekeeper via the revoked Emil Grigorov (WWB7JA7AQV) Developer ID. Rationale: Anchors on the exact first-stage executable name 'veltod' and the /Volumes-mounted Werkbit.app container named in the article and confirmed by Jamf (bundle dev.golove.velto). Renaming 'veltod' is caught by the Werkbit.app path clause. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-crashstealer-malware-poses-as-apple-crash-reporting-tool/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195278/malware/crashstealer-new-macos-infostealer-uses-signed-apps-to-evade-gatekeeper.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1553.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool coincidentally binary-named 'veltod' (extremely unlikely, non-dictionary name)
  • QA/malware-analysis workstation intentionally detonating the sample from a mounted DMG
  • Security researcher re-mounting a captured Werkbit.app for analysis
  • EDR sensor replaying archived process events during backfill
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mdworker","XProtect","VirusTotal")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the process image path is under /Volumes/Werkbit* or */Werkbit.app/* and pull the code-signing identity — Apple revoked the Emil Grigorov (WWB7JA7AQV) cert, so a valid-but-revoked signature confirms the sample. Note the mount source DMG and downloading user. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the veltod PID, unmount and quarantine the DMG, and force-expire the user's browser/keychain sessions. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host for a /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg drop, a new ~/Library/LaunchAgents plist, and outbound traffic to 179.43.166.242 or endpoint-api-v1.com to scope full-chain compromise.

| where FileName =~ "veltod"
   or (FolderPath has "Werkbit.app" and FolderPath has "/Volumes/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

CrashStealer C2 pull: veltod fetching sys.cache from GitHub + endpoint-api-v1.com AICommand & Control High
Hunts the CrashStealer second-stage retrieval where 'veltod' pulls 'sys.cache' from github/raw.githubusercontent.com (mgothiclove/pkeys) and the shell downloader reaches the delivery endpoint endpoint-api-v1[.]com/d/f1b24e, plus sibling campaign domains. Article-specific via the exact attacker-controlled domains and the anomalous veltod->GitHub egress. Rationale: endpoint-api-v1.com, cohezo.io/.com, cordinex.io and werkbit.io are attacker-registered domains confirmed by Jamf; the veltod->raw.githubusercontent.com clause catches the mgothiclove/pkeys dead-drop pull that legitimate software never performs. High fidelity because these domains have no benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://appleinsider.com/articles/26/07/13/crashstealer-malware-poses-as-an-apple-tool-to-steal-passwords-mac-data
ATT&CKT1105 T1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment or sandbox tooling actively resolving the IOC domains during analysis
  • Passive-DNS or scanner appliance sweeping the campaign domains
  • A benign process on the host querying github; note the detection requires veltod as the initiator for github, so this is filtered
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ logging the blocked resolution (still worth reviewing)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the resolving host and the initiating process; confirm whether the query is for a hardcoded campaign domain (endpoint-api-v1.com etc.) versus the veltod->github dead-drop. Check if resolution succeeded and any follow-on connection to 179.43.166.242. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block the campaign domains and 179.43.166.242 at egress, isolate the host if veltod or CrashReporter is present. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all endpoints for the same domain resolutions and for /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg and LaunchAgent persistence to find other PIN-gated victims.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("endpoint-api-v1.com","cohezo.io","cohezo.com","cordinex.io","werkbit.io")
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "veltod" and RemoteUrl has_any ("raw.githubusercontent.com","github.com"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("endpoint-api-v1.com","cohezo.io","cohezo.com","cordinex.io","werkbit.io")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DstIpAddr, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CrashStealer second-stage payload CrashReporter.dmg staged in /tmp AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the CrashStealer next-stage disk image 'CrashReporter.dmg' in /tmp (macOS /private/tmp) by the shell downloader script. Article-specific via the exact staged payload filename and temp-directory drop path that the veltod-invoked curl chain uses. Rationale: CrashReporter.dmg written to /tmp is the exact staged payload filename and path named in the article; a disk image landing in a world-writable temp dir from a downloader script is a high-signal, near-zero-benign event on macOS endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/crashstealer-macos-malware-uses.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer/CI job coincidentally building a disk image literally named CrashReporter.dmg into /tmp (rare; verify signer)
  • Crash-diagnostics tooling exporting an archive to tmp (would not typically be a .dmg named CrashReporter)
  • Malware-analysis lab detonating the sample
  • Backup/temp cleanup tools moving a previously dropped payload
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the writing process — a curl/sh/bash chain parented by veltod strongly confirms CrashStealer; capture the file hash and the source URL (endpoint-api-v1.com/d/f1b24e). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, quarantine /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg before it is mounted/executed, and terminate any veltod or downloader shell. Step 3 (hunt): Look for a mounted CrashReporter volume, a new LaunchAgent plist, keychain/browser credential access, and egress to 179.43.166.242.

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "CrashReporter.dmg"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/private/tmp/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

CrashStealer LaunchAgent persistence written by temp/DMG-resident process AIInstallation Medium
Hunts CrashStealer establishing persistence by writing a LaunchAgent plist into ~/Library/LaunchAgents from a process running out of /tmp, /private/tmp or a mounted /Volumes DMG (the CrashReporter/veltod stager that copies and re-signs itself). Article-specific via the temp/DMG-resident initiator writing the autostart plist. Rationale: Anchors LaunchAgent persistence (T1543.001) to the CrashStealer-specific initiator context — a stager running from /tmp, /private/tmp or a mounted DMG, or literally named veltod/CrashReporter — which separates it from the thousands of legitimate installers that also write LaunchAgents. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/macos-malware-apple-crash-reporter/
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1553.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A software installer temporarily extracting a helper into /private/tmp before registering a legitimate LaunchAgent
  • App run directly from a mounted DMG that installs its own auto-launch helper (e.g. some updater tools)
  • Homebrew/pkg post-install scripts writing agents from a temp working dir
  • MDM/config-management pushing a LaunchAgent via a staged temp payload
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("installer","package_script_service","munki","jamf") )
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the new plist and read the Program/ProgramArguments — a path pointing at a copied+re-signed CrashStealer binary (often in ~/Library or /tmp) confirms it; check the code signature (valid but revoked = CrashStealer). Step 2 (contain): Unload and delete the LaunchAgent (launchctl bootout), remove the referenced binary, isolate host. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with a preceding /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg drop, codesign invocations with -f/--force by the stager, and egress to 179.43.166.242 to confirm the full chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/"
| where FileName endswith ".plist"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/private/tmp/","/Volumes/")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veltod","CrashReporter")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceFileEvents

   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veltod","CrashReporter")

CrashStealer credential harvest: temp/DMG process reading keychain + browser/wallet stores AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the CrashStealer collection stage where a process running from /tmp, /private/tmp or a mounted DMG accesses the login keychain and Chromium/Firefox credential databases (Login Data, Cookies, key4.db, logins.json) plus wallet Local Extension Settings. Article-specific via the temp/DMG-resident non-browser initiator touching multiple credential stores. Rationale: CrashStealer harvests browsers, wallets, password managers and the login keychain; anchoring on a non-browser process from /tmp/DMG touching >=2 distinct credential stores (keychain + Chromium Login Data/Cookies/Firefox key4.db + wallet extension storage) yields a fan-out signal that legitimate single-app access does not produce. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/macos-stealer-mimics-apples-crash-report/
ATT&CKT1555.001 T1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate password manager or browser-import utility bulk-reading credential stores (filtered by excluding browser initiators and requiring a temp/DMG initiator)
  • Backup software (e.g. Time Machine helper) enumerating ~/Library
  • Forensic/DFIR collection tooling run from a mounted volume
  • Security product scanning keychain and browser profiles
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("1Password","Bitwarden","KeePassXC","backupd","mds","mdworker_shared")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and its path — a binary in /tmp or a mounted DMG (or named veltod/CrashReporter) reading login.keychain-db plus multiple browser stores confirms active harvesting. Note which browsers/wallets were touched. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, kill the process, and force credential rotation for the affected user: keychain/login password, browser-saved passwords, and any crypto wallet seed phrases immediately (assume wallet drain risk). Step 3 (hunt): Look for a subsequent ZIP archive written to a temp dir and outbound transfer to 179.43.166.242; scope other hosts for the same fan-out pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/private/tmp/","/Volumes/")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veltod","CrashReporter")
| where FileName in~ ("login.keychain-db","Login Data","Cookies","key4.db","logins.json")
   or FolderPath has_any ("/Local Extension Settings/","/Application Support/Exodus/","/Application Support/Ledger Live/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Google Chrome","firefox","Brave Browser","Microsoft Edge","com.apple.WebKit")
| summarize DistinctStores = dcount(FileName), Stores = make_set(FileName, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where DistinctStores >= 2   // >=2 distinct credential stores by one temp/DMG process = harvest fan-out
| order by LastSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/private/tmp/","/Volumes/")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veltod","CrashReporter")
| where FileName in~ ("login.keychain-db","Login Data","Cookies","key4.db","logins.json")
   or FolderPath has_any ("/Local Extension Settings/","/Application Support/Exodus/","/Application Support/Ledger Live/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Google Chrome","firefox","Brave Browser","Microsoft Edge","com.apple.WebKit")
| summarize DistinctStores = dcount(FileName), Stores = make_set(FileName, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where DistinctStores >= 2   // >=2 distinct credential stores by one temp/DMG process = harvest fan-out
| order by LastSeen desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| (TargetFileName=/(login\.keychain-db|Login Data|Cookies|key4\.db|logins\.json)$/i OR TargetFileName=/\/Local Extension Settings\//i)
| (ContextImageFileName=/\/(private\/)?tmp\//i OR ContextImageFileName=/^\/Volumes\//i OR ContextImageFileName=/\/(veltod|CrashReporter)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true), as=distinctStores)
| distinctStores >= 2

CrashStealer AES-GCM ZIP exfiltration to 179.43.166.242 over libcurl AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the CrashStealer exfiltration stage: outbound connection to the hardcoded attacker C2 179.43.166[.]242, which received the AES-GCM-encrypted ZIP of harvested browser/wallet/keychain data over libcurl. Article-specific via the exact C2 IP confirmed by Jamf (previously leaked in the app's ATS plist exception). Rationale: 179.43.166.242 is the hardcoded exfiltration C2 confirmed by Jamf (leaked via an ATS exception in an earlier build's plist) and reported by The Hacker News; any endpoint connecting to this IP is a direct data-theft indicator with essentially no benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195278/malware/crashstealer-new-macos-infostealer-uses-signed-apps-to-evade-gatekeeper.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1560.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or scanning infrastructure probing the C2 IP
  • A researcher/sandbox intentionally connecting to the IP for analysis
  • Shared-hosting reuse where the IP later serves benign content (verify timing vs. campaign window)
  • Proxy/NAT egress that aggregates many hosts behind one source — confirm the true internal originator
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the internal host and initiating process connecting to 179.43.166.242 and measure bytes_out — a spike indicates the ZIP was exfiltrated. Correlate with prior credential-store access on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Block 179.43.166.242 at the perimeter, isolate the host, and treat all local credentials (keychain, browser passwords, crypto wallet seeds, password-manager vaults) as compromised — rotate immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all endpoints for connections to this IP and the campaign domains (endpoint-api-v1.com, cohezo.io/.com, cordinex.io, werkbit.io), and for the CrashReporter.dmg/LaunchAgent artifacts to enumerate the full victim set.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "179.43.166.242"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "179.43.166.242"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, ApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc
