DIRAC ReqManager service (CVE-2026-45579) spawning a shell or recon/egress binary AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payload executing: the DIRAC RequestManager service (a Python DB-facing handler launched via dirac-service/dirac-tornado as ReqManager/TornadoReqManager) spawning /bin/sh, bash or a recon/egress tool. The eval() on the unrecognised groupingAttribute walks back to the os module, so successful exploitation manifests as this DB service forking a shell — something ReqManager never does legitimately (unlike RequestExecutingAgent, which forks a ProcessPool). Rationale: Anchored on the ReqManager/ReqManagerHandler/dirac-service parent identity (DIRAC docs: ReqManager is the DB-facing handler that never shells out) combined with any shell/recon/egress child — the exact tree the eval()->os.* chain from the advisory produces. Parent token deliberately excludes RequestExecutingAgent, which forks a legitimate ProcessPool. Datadog/Falcon left empty: their provided auditd/ProcessRollup2 schemas expose no parent command line to key the DIRAC-service parent on (only ParentBaseFileName='python', too generic). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-45579/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9jpv-c7p4-997x • https://dirac.diracgrid.org/en/latest/AdministratorGuide/Systems/RequestManagement/rmsComponents.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC administrator running diagnostic shell commands under the runit/supervisor process tree during service troubleshooting
  • Container entrypoint/init wrapper spawning a shell during a dirac-service (re)start
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet/Salt) restarting dirac-tornado and running post-restart health-check shell hooks
  • Site monitoring probes (monit/nagios) that shell out from the service supervisor
  • A local health-check script using curl/nc to poll the ReqManager port on service start
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has "healthcheck" and ChildCmd !has "/opt/dirac/pro/versions" and ChildCmd !has "runsvdir"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child command line and SHA256; correlate against the ReqManager log for the exception traceback the advisory says the exploit leaves (NameError/AttributeError referencing 'Request.' or dunder strings such as __class__/__globals__/__builtins__), and identify the authenticated user whose RPC to getRequestCountersWeb preceded it. 2) Contain: isolate the DIRAC host, rotate all secrets in dirac.cfg (database passwords) and revoke every stored proxy/token, then upgrade DIRAC to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 3) Hunt: search the same host for reads of dirac.cfg by non-DIRAC processes, outbound egress from the service, and truncation/deletion of the RequestManager log (evidence removal noted in the advisory).

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","id","whoami","hostname","uname","cat","base64","chmod")

| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DIRAC post-exploit read of dirac.cfg by a shell/read utility (CVE-2026-45579 credential theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-theft step the advisory describes: after the eval() RCE, the attacker reads the local dirac.cfg to harvest database passwords and export stored proxies/tokens. Keys on a read/exfil utility (cat, grep, base64, curl, etc.) whose own command line references dirac.cfg — excluding the Python DIRAC service that carries dirac.cfg as a legitimate --cfg argument. Rationale: Keys on dirac.cfg (the file the advisory names as holding DB passwords and gating proxy/token export) appearing in the command line of a read/exfil utility rather than the Python service. The reader-binary allowlist excludes the legitimate DIRAC process, which carries dirac.cfg as a --cfg argument — so any cat/grep/base64/curl of dirac.cfg is anomalous. Portable across all process-telemetry platforms because it keys on the executing process's own command line. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-45579/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9jpv-c7p4-997x

  • Config-management tooling templating or diffing dirac.cfg on each run
  • Monitoring/inventory scripts grepping dirac.cfg for a version or option value
  • Site install/upgrade scripts copying dirac.cfg with scp/curl to a new node

and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent of the reader process — if it descends from the DIRAC service (dirac-service/dirac-tornado/ReqManager) rather than an interactive admin shell, treat as confirmed exploitation; check whether the command pipes to base64/curl/nc (exfil) and whether stored proxy/token files were touched. 2) Contain: isolate the host, immediately rotate every credential in dirac.cfg and revoke all stored user proxies and tokens, and patch DIRAC to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 3) Hunt: pivot on the authenticated user who called getRequestCountersWeb, review the ReqManager log for the eval exception traceback, and look for outbound transfers of dirac.cfg / proxy material and any subsequent log truncation.

Google and Microsoft Pull ModHeader With 1.6 Million Installs After Dormant Collector Found

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Google and Microsoft have pulled ModHeader, a popular header-editing extension with roughly 1.6 million installs across Chrome and Edge, after researchers found a hidden browsing-history collector built into its official store version. The collector was dormant. An empty allow-list kept it switched off, and no proof has emerged that it ever gathered or sent a single browsing domain. The

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanised ModHeader extension ID (idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj) present on host · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ModHeader collector callback to stanfordstudies.com / extensions-hub.com · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ModHeader browsing-history exfil POST to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
ModHeader collector callback to stanfordstudies.com / extensions-hub.com AICommand & Control High
Hunts host resolution and network connections to the two domains hardwired into the trojanised ModHeader extension: extensions-hub.com (pinged on install/update/uninstall, confirmed active) and api.stanfordstudies.com (the dormant daily browsing-history exfil endpoint). Because the browser process itself makes the call, the connection is attributed to chrome.exe/msedge.exe. Rationale: Both domains are named directly in the article and corroborated by Yunus Aydın and HackIndex teardowns; extensions-hub.com fires on every install/update/uninstall (confirmed active), making this a reliable trip-wire even though the browsing-history exfil path is gated off. Cross-checked against: • https://aydinnyunus.github.io/2026/07/12/modheader-data-exfiltration-stanfordstudies/ • https://hackindex.io/research/modheader-malware-chrome-spyware • https://gbhackers.com/modheader-chrome-extension-exposes-900000-users/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-registered but similarly-named advertising domain sharing the extensions-hub.com string in a subdomain
  • Security researchers or the SOC intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox VM
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving the IOC domains for verdict lookups
  • A proxy/DNS-security appliance's own IOC-testing beacon
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser (chrome.exe/msedge.exe) and check whether the host has the ModHeader extension ID idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj on disk (see the extension-inventory UC). 2) CONTAIN: Block stanfordstudies.com and extensions-hub.com at DNS and proxy; push removal of the ModHeader extension and verify no managed-extension policy / profile-sync will reinstall it. 3) HUNT: If the host also beaconed to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log, treat the collector as activated — pull proxy logs for the POST body size and rotate any API keys / bearer tokens / session cookies the user pasted into ModHeader's header history.

| where RemoteUrl has_any ("stanfordstudies.com", "extensions-hub.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), SampleUrl=any(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("stanfordstudies.com", "extensions-hub.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count() by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

Trojanised ModHeader extension ID (idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj) present on host AIInstallation High
Inventories hosts where the pulled ModHeader extension is (or was) installed by matching its Chrome/Edge Web Store extension ID in the on-disk extension directory. This finds the affected population regardless of whether the dormant collector ever fired, so you can drive removal and secret-rotation. Rationale: The extension ID idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj is the single most durable IOC in the article — it is fixed, unique to the pulled build, and appears in the browser's on-disk extension directory whether or not the collector activated, giving a clean affected-host inventory. 1) TRIAGE: Confirm the extension directory is live (not an archived/backup copy) and identify the browser profile owner. 2) CONTAIN: Force-remove the extension from Chrome and Edge, then verify no ExtensionInstallForcelist GPO/Intune policy or profile-sync will reinstall it; uninstalling clears its stored data. 3) HUNT: Cross-reference these hosts against the collector-callback UC; for any user who used ModHeader's header-history feature, rotate API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies, since full HTTP headers were stored on disk in plaintext.

ModHeader browsing-history exfil POST to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log AIActions on Objectives High
Targets the collector's activated exfiltration path specifically: an HTTP POST to api.stanfordstudies.com with the URI /app/log, which uploads the encrypted domain list plus device fingerprint before wiping the local copy. Requires web-proxy/gateway telemetry that captures URI and method, so it distinguishes real exfil from the dormant-state domain resolution. Rationale: The article and Yunus Aydın's teardown both name the exact upload target — a POST to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log carrying the encrypted domain list and fingerprint — so matching host+method+URI on proxy logs is a high-fidelity signal that the dormant collector has actually been switched on. Cross-checked against: • https://aydinnyunus.github.io/2026/07/12/modheader-data-exfiltration-stanfordstudies/ • https://cyberpress.org/modheader-chrome-extension-exposes-900000/

  • A DLP/CASB solution replaying the request for inspection
  • Threat-intel tooling probing the endpoint for a live-verdict check
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the POST targeted api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log from a browser process and note SentBytes — a non-trivial body means the encrypted domain list was uploaded. 2) CONTAIN: Sinkhole/block stanfordstudies.com at DNS and proxy, remove the ModHeader extension from the host, and isolate if body size indicates bulk upload. 3) HUNT: This confirms the allow-list was populated (collector active) — sweep all hosts with the extension ID for the same POST, and rotate every secret (API keys, bearer tokens, session cookies) the affected users pasted into ModHeader's header-history feature, which stored full HTTP headers in plaintext on disk.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm maintainer credential-phish lookalike domain npmjs.help (chalk/debug ATO)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — What is a dependency firewall?
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] plain-crypto-js postinstall RAT dropper spawns downloader (axios/Sapphire Sleet) · [LLM] axios RAT dropped artifacts: renamed PowerShell wt.exe + campaign 6202033 files · [LLM] axios RAT persistence: HKCU Run value MicrosoftUpdate pointing to system.bat · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] axios RAT C2 beacon to sfrclak[.]com / 142.11.206.73:8000 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Malicious postmark-mcp BCC email exfiltration to phan@giftshop[.]club · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
npm maintainer credential-phish lookalike domain npmjs.help (chalk/debug ATO) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/web contact to the lookalike domain npmjs.help, the fake '2FA reset' phishing site used to steal the npm maintainer credentials behind the September 2025 chalk/debug supply-chain compromise. Legitimate npm lives on npmjs.com/npmjs.org, so any hit on npmjs.help is a maintainer-targeted credential-phishing indicator. Rationale: npmjs.help is a confirmed lookalike phishing domain (registered 2025-09-05, three days pre-attack) named in the article and corroborated by Sygnia/Checkmarx/Cycode/Aikido as the credential-theft vector for the chalk/debug ATO. Exact-domain match against a domain with no legitimate use = high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-debug-and-chalk-packages-compromised • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/npm-supply-chain-attack-september-2025/ • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/chalk-and-17-other-npm-packages-compromised-in-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or TI platform detonating/browsing npmjs.help in a sandboxed research VM
  • Automated URL-enrichment (SOAR/secure-web-gateway) resolving the domain for reputation scoring
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platform hosting a lookalike test page
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the blocked query
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user that resolved npmjs.help and whether a browser or npm tooling initiated it; pull any credential-entry or npm login activity in the following 30 min. 2) Contain: force-reset the affected npm account credentials and revoke/rotate npm publish tokens and 2FA; block npmjs.help at the proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: check whether that maintainer published any npm package versions after the resolution timestamp, and scan lockfiles/CI for the chalk/debug malicious versions and browser-side crypto-address-swapping payloads.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "npmjs.help"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "npmjs.help"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

plain-crypto-js postinstall RAT dropper spawns downloader (axios/Sapphire Sleet) AIInstallation High
Hunts the malicious plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 postinstall (setup.js) hook — pulled in transitively by axios@1.14.1/0.30.4 — spawning a downloader/interpreter that references the RAT campaign artifacts (sfrclak C2, campaign ID 6202033) to fetch platform-specific payloads. Targets the exact execution behaviour Microsoft attributes to Sapphire Sleet. Rationale: sfrclak, 142.11.206.73, campaign ID 6202033 and the plain-crypto-js dependency name are Datadog/Elastic/Socket-confirmed IOCs for the March 2026 axios RAT dropper (setup.js postinstall). These strings do not appear in benign build output, making a command-line match high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in a lab (command lines will legitimately contain the IOCs)
  • IR/hunt scripts that embed the IOC strings as search arguments in their own command lines
  • Threat-intel simulation/purple-team replay of the axios TTPs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("windbg.exe","procmon.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("MALWARE-LAB","SANDBOX"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain (node.exe/npm → interpreter) and whether the host has axios 1.14.1/0.30.4 or plain-crypto-js 4.2.1 in node_modules/lockfiles. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the RAT chain, and block sfrclak[.]com + 142.11.206.73 at egress. 3) Hunt: sweep for the dropped artifacts (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe, system.bat, %TEMP%\6202033.ps1/.vbs, /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond, /tmp/ld.py), the MicrosoftUpdate Run key, and beacons to the C2; rotate any dev/CI credentials on the machine.

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","curl.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","osascript","bash","sh")

| order by Timestamp desc

| where CommandLine has_any ("sfrclak","6202033","plain-crypto-js","142.11.206.73")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT dropped artifacts: renamed PowerShell wt.exe + campaign 6202033 files AIInstallation High
Hunts file-system writes of the axios/plain-crypto-js RAT's dropped payloads across OSes: a renamed PowerShell (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe), the persistence script system.bat, VBScript/PS1 droppers named 6202033, the macOS fake Apple daemon com.apple.act.mond, and the Linux payload ld.py. These paths are masquerading indicators unique to the Sapphire Sleet RAT staging. Rationale: The dropped paths (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe = renamed PowerShell, system.bat, %TEMP%\6202033.ps1/.vbs, /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond, /tmp/ld.py) are verbatim IOCs from Datadog/Elastic write-ups. Excluding \WindowsApps\ removes the legitimate Windows Terminal wt.exe, leaving only the masqueraded copy. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Windows Terminal wt.exe (lives under \WindowsApps\, excluded by the filter)
  • An admin/backup script legitimately named system.bat deployed via GPO to ProgramData
  • A developer repo on macOS/Linux containing an unrelated ld.py linker helper
  • EDR sample-collection/quarantine copying the artifact into a scan folder
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\WindowsApps\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (should trace back to node.exe/npm postinstall) and hash the dropped file against the published SHA-256s (e.g. Windows PS payload 617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101). 2) Contain: isolate host, delete artifacts, remove the MicrosoftUpdate Run key, block sfrclak[.]com/142.11.206.73. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same InitiatingProcess across the fleet, and audit npm lockfiles org-wide for axios 1.14.1/0.30.4 and plain-crypto-js 4.2.1.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "wt.exe" and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or (FileName =~ "system.bat" and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or FileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1")
   or FileName =~ "com.apple.act.mond"
   or FileName =~ "ld.py"
| where FolderPath !has @"\WindowsApps\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "wt.exe" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or (TargetFileName =~ "system.bat" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1","com.apple.act.mond","ld.py")
| where TargetFilePath !has @"\WindowsApps\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT persistence: HKCU Run value MicrosoftUpdate pointing to system.bat AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact autostart persistence set by the axios/plain-crypto-js RAT: an HKCU CurrentVersion\Run value named 'MicrosoftUpdate' whose data references system.bat, re-executing the payload at each logon. The masqueraded value name plus the system.bat data string make this a tight, single-event persistence signal. Rationale: The Run value name 'MicrosoftUpdate' -> system.bat is the exact persistence IOC documented by Datadog for the axios RAT. Value-name masquerading as a Microsoft component combined with a .bat data string is a precise, low-noise autostart indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal update tool that (poorly) names its Run value MicrosoftUpdate and points to a .bat wrapper
  • Sysadmin logon automation deployed via a system.bat referenced in a Run key
  • Software packaging/testing that seeds throwaway Run keys
  • Golden-image build tooling writing autostart entries
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the writing process and the full RegistryValueData path; confirm whether it points to %PROGRAMDATA%\system.bat. 2) Contain: remove the Run value, delete system.bat and the renamed wt.exe, isolate the host, block the C2. 3) Hunt: query the fleet for the same value name/data pair, correlate to hosts that recently ran npm installs of axios/plain-crypto-js, and check egress logs for sfrclak[.]com beacons on port 8000.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "MicrosoftUpdate"
| where RegistryValueData has "system.bat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "MicrosoftUpdate"
| where RegistryValueData has "system.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT C2 beacon to sfrclak[.]com / 142.11.206.73:8000 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint DNS/network contact to the axios RAT command-and-control infrastructure sfrclak[.]com and 142.11.206.73 (payload URL http://sfrclak[.]com:8000/6202033, 60-second beacon loop). Single-indicator network match against dedicated, freshly registered attacker infrastructure. Rationale: sfrclak[.]com (registered 2026-03-30) and 142.11.206.73:8000 are the Datadog/Elastic-confirmed C2 for the axios RAT. Dedicated attacker infrastructure with no legitimate use yields a near-zero-FP network detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/axios-supply-chain-attack-pushes-cross.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TI enrichment/sandbox host resolving sfrclak[.]com for reputation scoring
  • Security researcher pcap replay of the campaign
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ logging the query it just blocked
  • Passive-DNS collector mirroring the domain
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the beaconing process (expect powershell/python/curl descended from node) and beacon cadence (~60s). 2) Contain: isolate host, block sfrclak[.]com + 142.11.206.73 at the firewall/proxy, kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for any resolution of sfrclak[.]com, correlate to recent axios/plain-crypto-js installs and the MicrosoftUpdate Run-key persistence, and rotate credentials cached on impacted hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "sfrclak.com" or RemoteIP == "142.11.206.73"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = SourceIP, SrcHostname = SourceHostName, Indicator = strcat(DestinationIP, " ", DestinationHostName))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious postmark-mcp BCC email exfiltration to phan@giftshop[.]club AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound mail silently BCC'd to phan@giftshop[.]club, the exfiltration address hard-coded into the trojanised postmark-mcp@1.0.16 npm MCP server (the first confirmed malicious MCP server on npm). Any recipient in the giftshop.club domain on org mail flow is a direct exfiltration indicator. Rationale: phan@giftshop[.]club is the verbatim BCC exfiltration address added in postmark-mcp@1.0.16, corroborated by Snyk/The Register/The Hacker News. It matches the article's pre-extracted IOC giftshop.club; any org mail with a giftshop.club recipient is high-fidelity exfiltration. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/first-malicious-mcp-server-found.html • https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/29/postmark_mcp_server_code_hijacked/
ATT&CKT1114 T1020 T1195.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine business contact who happens to use a giftshop.club address (verify domain legitimacy first)
  • A phishing/threat-intel test message deliberately addressed to the IOC domain
  • Mail-security detonation/replay tooling re-sending a captured malicious message
  • A distribution-list expansion that legitimately contains the address (should be treated as compromise, not FP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all messages with a giftshop.club recipient, note the sending mailboxes/service principals and whether the send path involved an MCP server or automation. 2) Contain: block giftshop.club at mail flow, purge outbound copies, and audit dev workstations for the postmark-mcp npm package (any version >=1.0.16); remove it. 3) Hunt: inventory MCP servers/AI-agent tooling pulling from npm, review what those agents had access to (email, secrets), and rotate any credentials the exposed emails may have contained.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RecipientEmailAddress endswith "giftshop.club" or SenderFromDomain =~ "giftshop.club"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, EmailDirection, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "Exchange"
| where Recipients has "giftshop.club" or P2RecipientList has "giftshop.club"
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, ClientIP, Recipients, P2RecipientList
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" OR All_Email.recipient="phan@giftshop.club") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

New MemGhost Attack Plants Persistent False Memories in AI Agents Through One Email

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 3 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

Give an AI assistant a memory and access to your inbox, and you hand an attacker a way to rewrite what it thinks it knows about you. A single email can trick that agent into saving a false "fact" about the user, hide the change, and quietly steer its answers in later sessions. When it works, the person reads an ordinary-looking reply and never learns their assistant was tampered with. The

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound email followed within minutes by agent memory-file write (MemGhost one-email chain)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Writes to AI-agent persistent memory/instruction files (AGENTS.md, MEMORY.md) — MemGhost poisoning artifact
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Writes to AI-agent persistent memory/instruction files (AGENTS.md, MEMORY.md) — MemGhost poisoning artifact AIInstallation Low
Hunts file create/modify events on the exact plaintext state files OpenClaw and Claude Code SDK agents load into model context every session (AGENTS.md standing instructions, MEMORY.md learned facts). MemGhost's whole persistence mechanism is a single write into these core files so the false 'fact' reloads in every later session; logging and reviewing every write to them is the researchers' own recommended defense. Rationale: AGENTS.md and MEMORY.md are the exact core state files named in the article and paper as the poisoning target (loaded every session); the researchers explicitly recommend logging every write to these files, making a file-event hunt the highest-fidelity article-grounded pivot. Cross-checked the arXiv paper and EchoLeak advisory for the same email-borne AI-memory pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/html/2607.05189v1 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-memghost-attack-plants-persistent.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-32711
ATT&CKT1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal agent operation legitimately updating MEMORY.md as it learns real user preferences
  • Developer manually editing AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md in an IDE (VS Code, Notepad++)
  • git clone/checkout of agent-template repositories that ship an AGENTS.md
  • Agent framework upgrade rewriting default AGENTS.md scaffolding
  • Backup/sync tooling (OneDrive, Dropbox) rewriting the files on restore
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","Code.exe","devenv.exe","notepad.exe","notepad++.exe","OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the current AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md and its version/backup history; look for injected authorization or financial claims (e.g. a raised Zelle/transfer limit like the paper's $10,000 test lure) or instructions to stay silent about the change. 2) Contain: snapshot the file for evidence, revert to a known-good copy, and disable the agent's autonomous email-triggered / background runs until reviewed. 3) Hunt: correlate the write time against recently delivered inbound email to that user (hidden/agent-directed text), and sweep other agent hosts for writes to the same two filenames.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where FileName in~ ("MEMORY.md","AGENTS.md")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Writes=count(), Paths=make_set(FolderPath,5)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("MEMORY.md","AGENTS.md")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Writes=count(), Paths=make_set(TargetFilePath,5)
    by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
title: AI Agent Persistent Memory File Written (MemGhost stealth memory injection)
id: 6f3a1e42-2c7b-4d19-9a8e-3f0b7c9d1a55
description: Detects create/modify of OpenClaw / Claude Code SDK persistent state files (AGENTS.md, MEMORY.md) that are loaded into model context each session and are the target of MemGhost email-borne memory poisoning.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-memghost-attack-plants-persistent.html
  - https://arxiv.org/html/2607.05189v1
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1565.001
  - attack.impact
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\MEMORY.md'
      - '\AGENTS.md'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate agent memory updates during normal user conversation
  - Developers editing AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md by hand or via git checkout
level: low
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\MEMORY.md OR *\\memory.md OR *\\AGENTS.md OR *\\agents.md)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\(MEMORY|AGENTS)\.md$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` 
| where user!="" AND NOT match(user,"\$$") 
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` 
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` 
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="MEMORY.md" OR Filesystem.file_name="AGENTS.md") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_id

| sort - lastTime
Inbound email followed within minutes by agent memory-file write (MemGhost one-email chain) AIDelivery Low
Temporal correlation targeting MemGhost's signature: a single inbound email reaches a mailbox an AI agent reads, and within a short window the agent writes AGENTS.md or MEMORY.md on that user's endpoint. Ties the delivery (initial access) to the persistence write so the analyst sees the one-shot email-to-false-memory pivot rather than either event in isolation. Rationale: Uses the article's core claim — one inbound email causes the agent to write its persistent memory (AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md) — as a delivery-to-persistence temporal join on the recipient's UPN, which is the MemGhost fingerprint no single-event rule captures. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because the email half depends on Defender XDR EmailEvents with no equivalent in those tenants; the file half alone would duplicate UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/html/2607.05189v1 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-memghost-attack-plants-persistent.html
ATT&CKT1566 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Email.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User receives a legitimate email and, in the same session, chats with the agent causing a genuine memory update within 30 minutes
  • Newsletter/automation mail arriving coincidentally near a routine agent memory refresh
  • Agent processing a legitimate task email that legitimately updates a stored preference
  • Shared mailbox where email recipient UPN and endpoint user coincide by chance
  • Developer testing the agent's email skill with benign messages
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the correlated email (SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId) and inspect its raw body for hidden/agent-directed instructions (HTML comments, white-on-white text, memory-write or stay-silent directives); diff the AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md write for injected authorization/financial facts. 2) Contain: quarantine the message across mailboxes, revert the poisoned memory file, and suspend the agent's inbox-reading/background automation. 3) Hunt: search EmailEvents for the same sender/cluster to other agent users, and re-run UC1 across all hosts running OpenClaw or Claude Code SDK agents for further AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md writes.
let Window = 30m;
let Mail = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | project MailTime=Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where FileName in~ ("MEMORY.md","AGENTS.md")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountUpn)
| join kind=inner Mail on $left.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| where Timestamp between (MailTime .. MailTime + Window)
| project MailTime, WriteTime=Timestamp,
          DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, MailTime),
          DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId
| order by WriteTime desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let Window = 30m;
let Mail = EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | project MailTime=TimeGenerated, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId;
DeviceFileEvents

| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

          DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId
| order by WriteTime desc

Forg365 PhaaS Targets Microsoft 365 with Device Code and AitM Session Theft

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 13 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A new phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) operation called Forg365 is using a combination of device code phishing, adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) tactics, antibot evasion, artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted lure creation, and post-compromise mailbox operations targeting Microsoft 365 accounts. Distributed via Telegram and costing $400 a month (or $3,800 per year), attack chains leverage phishing

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Forg365 phishing email: Amazon SES sender with SendGrid/logfriend redirect link · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] First-seen Entra device-code auth via Microsoft Authentication Broker (Forg365) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OAuth consent grant to app with mailbox permissions post-device-code (Forg365 persistence) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Broker device-code sign-in from Node.js automation UA (Forg365 operator backend) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] M365 broker token replay from anomalous country after interactive login (AitM/ForgCookie) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
First-seen Entra device-code auth via Microsoft Authentication Broker (Forg365) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a user's first successful device-code sign-in bound to the Microsoft Authentication Broker first-party app (29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e), the exact client Forg365's device-auth branch pushes victims into. A single successful redemption yields tokens across Exchange, Graph, OneDrive and SharePoint, so a first-time broker auth per user is a high-value takeover signal. Rationale: Anchors on the exact first-party AppId (29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) the article names as the 'legitimate Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in flow' Forg365 pushes victims into; the 45-day per-user baseline anti-join turns a noisy first-party app into a first-time-observed takeover signal. Cross-checked against: • https://zerobec.com/blog/inside-forg365-telegram-distributed-sneaky2fa-style-phaas • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-forg365-phishing-platform-uses-ai-to-target-microsoft-365-accounts/ • https://detection.fyi/elastic/detection-rules/integrations/azure/initial_access_entra_id_device_code_auth_with_broker_client/ • https://www.esentire.com/blog/tycoon-2fa-operators-adopt-oauth-device-code-phishing
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Azure CLI / Az PowerShell / Microsoft device-code login on new engineer workstations
  • First-time BYOD or Intune device registration through the Authentication Broker
  • Conference-room / shared IoT device enrollment using the device-code grant
  • Help-desk-assisted new-device onboarding for a user who hasn't used device code in 45 days
  • Airgapped/kiosk provisioning where interactive browser auth isn't available
Suppression filter
| where ResourceDisplayName !in ("Device Registration Service","Microsoft Device Registration Client")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the AccountUpn's sign-in IP/ASN/UserAgent and confirm whether the device-code request originated from a corporate egress and a known device; check for a matching help-desk/onboarding ticket. 2) Contain: if unrecognised, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset + re-MFA, and enable a Conditional Access policy blocking device-code flow for the user/group. 3) Hunt: enumerate all tokens issued to the broker app for this user, review mailbox for new inbox rules / forwarding, and pivot to UC4 (token replay) and UC5 (consent grants) for the same account.

Broker device-code sign-in from Node.js automation UA (Forg365 operator backend) AICommand & Control High
Hunts successful sign-ins to the Microsoft Authentication Broker app carrying Node.js/HTTP-library user agents (node, undici, axios). Forg365's server-side operator backend polls the device-code token endpoint programmatically, so a broker sign-in with a scripted UA — rather than a real browser/OS client — fingerprints the PhaaS automation rather than the victim's browser. Rationale: The node/undici user-agent against the broker AppId is a direct fingerprint of the Forg365 Node.js operator backend (confirmed by second-source device-code research); no legitimate victim signs into the broker with an HTTP-library UA, making this far higher fidelity than the raw device-code signal. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/forg365-phaas-abuses-microsoft-device-code-flow/ • https://www.esentire.com/blog/tycoon-2fa-operators-adopt-oauth-device-code-phishing • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/entra-id-oauth-phishing-detection
ATT&CKT1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • In-house Node.js/Python automation that legitimately performs device-code auth against the broker (rare)
  • Security or licensing tools that use MSAL Node to enumerate device state
  • Developer SDK testing of MSAL device-code samples
  • SIEM/SOAR connectors polling Graph via the broker client with a library UA
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the UserAgent and source ASN — library UAs from a hosting/VPS ASN (not a corporate range) is near-certain malicious; check whether the same AccountUpn also had a legitimate interactive broker auth minutes earlier (device-code completion). 2) Contain: revoke sign-in sessions and refresh tokens for the account, block the source IP/ASN, and disable device-code flow via Conditional Access. 3) Hunt: sweep all users showing broker sign-ins from the same source IP/ASN or identical library UA to scope the campaign, then check each mailbox for keyword-alert rules and AI-drafted replies.

Forg365 phishing email: Amazon SES sender with SendGrid/logfriend redirect link AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound delivered mail sent through Amazon SES infrastructure whose body links traverse SendGrid tracking hosts or land on the Forg365 operator domain logfriend.com. This mirrors the article's exact delivery pattern — SES-delivered lure, SendGrid-hosted images/tracking, redirection chain ending in Forg365-controlled domains — rather than generic phishing. Rationale: Combines the three delivery IOCs the article gives verbatim — Amazon SES envelope sender (amazonses.com), SendGrid-hosted tracking resources (sendgrid.net), and the Forg365 operator domain logfriend.com — so the SES+SendGrid+logfriend triple keys on this campaign rather than SES abuse in general. Cross-checked against: • https://zerobec.com/blog/inside-forg365-telegram-distributed-sneaky2fa-style-phaas • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-forg365-phishing-platform-uses-ai-to-target-microsoft-365-accounts/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SaaS newsletters/receipts sent via Amazon SES that also embed SendGrid tracking pixels
  • Marketing automation platforms that chain SES delivery with SendGrid click-tracking links
  • A partner using logfriend.com legitimately (verify domain reputation before assuming malicious)
  • Transactional mail (password resets, invoices) from vendors using SES egress ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: expand UrlChain / redirect for the flagged message and confirm whether the terminal host is a device-code or spoofed M365 login page; check how many recipients received the same NetworkMessageId cluster. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message org-wide (Search-Mailbox / purge), block logfriend.com and the SES sending domain at the mail gateway and proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate recipients against UC1/UC2 (broker device-code sign-ins) within 24h to find any recipient who clicked and authenticated; report the SES sending identity to AWS abuse.
let SesMail = EmailEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam") | where SenderMailFromDomain endswith "amazonses.com" or SenderFromDomain endswith "amazonses.com"; SesMail | join kind=inner (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId | where UrlDomain has_any ("sendgrid.net","logfriend.com") or Url has_any ("logfriend.com","sendgrid") | project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, NetworkMessageId | order by Timestamp desc

M365 broker token replay from anomalous country after interactive login (AitM/ForgCookie) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a user's recent interactive successful sign-in against a non-interactive Microsoft Authentication Broker token use from a different country within 12 hours. This targets Forg365's AitM session theft and the ForgCookie extension's silent-OAuth refresh, where a stolen token/cookie is replayed from attacker infrastructure while the legitimate user is active elsewhere. Rationale: Ties the article's AitM session theft and ForgCookie 'silent OAuth refresh' to observable telemetry: a non-interactive broker token used from a country different from the user's live interactive session within 12h is the network-shape signature of token/cookie replay from attacker infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://zerobec.com/blog/inside-forg365-telegram-distributed-sneaky2fa-style-phaas • https://www.esentire.com/blog/tycoon-2fa-operators-adopt-oauth-device-code-phishing
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate VPN or cloud egress that geolocates to a different country than the user's physical location
  • Traveling users whose mobile client refreshes tokens from an in-transit/border location
  • Roaming users with split-tunnel where broker refresh egresses via a different regional POP
  • Satellite/ISP CGNAT geo-IP misattribution
  • Legitimate cross-region SaaS connector acting on the user's behalf
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the two IP/ASNs — a hosting/VPS or residential-proxy ASN for the non-interactive token use (vs a mobile/ISP for the interactive) confirms replay; check the token's ResourceDisplayName for mailbox/OneDrive access. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens and sessions for the user, force re-auth, and if ForgCookie is suspected, isolate the endpoint and clear/rotate browser session state. 3) Hunt: review the account's mailbox for new inbox rules, keyword alerts, or AI-drafted thread replies, and check OneDrive/SharePoint access from the anomalous ASN; pivot the ASN across all users to scope the AitM campaign.

OAuth consent grant to app with mailbox permissions post-device-code (Forg365 persistence) AIInstallation Low
Hunts consent grants that delegate mailbox/offline permissions (Mail.Read, Mail.ReadWrite, Mail.Send, offline_access) to applications, aligning with Forg365's panel 'OAuth app configuration' and token-vaulting features used to retain access to compromised M365 mailboxes. Surfaces the persistence step where a stolen session is converted into a durable app grant. Rationale: Grounded in the article's operator-panel features (OAuth app configuration, token vaulting, browser-extension support) that convert a compromised session into durable mailbox access; scopes to consent events that grant Mail/offline_access delegated scopes rather than all consents. Cross-checked against: • https://zerobec.com/blog/inside-forg365-telegram-distributed-sneaky2fa-style-phaas • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/entra-id-oauth-phishing-detection
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin-approved deployment of a new mail-integrated SaaS app (e.g. e-signature, CRM, backup)
  • User self-service consent to a well-known productivity add-in
  • Approved migration/journaling tooling requesting Mail.Read
  • Marketplace apps onboarded during a sanctioned project
  • Re-consent after a permission version bump on an existing trusted app
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the consented app's publisher/ID and reputation, who consented, and from what IP; broad delegated Mail+offline_access on a first-seen or unverified-publisher app is high-risk. 2) Contain: revoke the service principal's grants (Remove-MgOauth2PermissionGrant), disable the enterprise app, and revoke the granting user's sessions. 3) Hunt: check Graph/mailbox activity by that app (bulk mail reads, sends, new inbox rules), correlate the consenting user with UC1/UC4 device-code and token-replay hits, and review all recent consents to the same app across the tenant.
CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where ActionType in ("Consent to application","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant","Add delegated permission grant") | where RawEventData has_any ("Mail.Read","Mail.ReadWrite","Mail.Send","MailboxSettings.ReadWrite","offline_access","User.Read.All") | project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, ApplicationId, RawEventData | order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where OperationName in ("Consent to application","Add delegated permission grant","Add app role assignment grant to user","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant") | extend TR = tostring(TargetResources) | where TR has_any ("Mail.Read","Mail.ReadWrite","Mail.Send","MailboxSettings.ReadWrite","offline_access","User.Read.All") | extend Actor = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName) | project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, Result, TargetResources | order by TimeGenerated desc
