title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command

Bulk PowerShell/net.exe Active Directory enumeration (Get-AD* cmdlet flurry) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the vibe-coded AD mapping stage: a burst of AD-discovery cmdlets (Get-ADUser/Computer/Group/OU/Trust, DirectorySearcher, nltest) or net group/user queries from a single interactive user session in a short window. Article-specific because the script harvested users, computers, groups, OUs and trusts in one aggressive pass rather than the one-off lookups admins run. Rationale: Anchored on the article's stated behaviour (mapping users, computers, groups, OUs and trusts) via the exact AD cmdlets/net commands, gated by a 5-min burst threshold to separate the aggressive one-pass harvest from routine admin lookups. Cross-checked Huntress blog and CyberSecurityNews. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vibe-coded-powershell-script-active-directory/
ATT&CKT1087.002 T1059.001 T1482
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tier-2 admin running an AD audit/BloodHound-style inventory legitimately
  • PingCastle / PurpleKnight AD assessment tooling
  • Logon script or SCCM/Intune inventory job invoking Get-AD cmdlets
  • Helpdesk bulk offboarding script querying net user/net group
  • Backup or IAM reconciliation jobs enumerating groups
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("svc-adaudit","svc-sccm") and not (Cmds has "BloodHound" or Cmds has "PingCastle")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating account is not a sanctioned AD-admin/service account and review the make_set of command lines for breadth (users AND computers AND trusts = mapping, not a lookup); check the host's logon type and source IP. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, disable the account, kill the PowerShell/net session, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for AD_Report.html or CSV writes in C:\ProgramData, and for follow-on s5cmd.exe / SharpShares.exe execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-ADUser","Get-ADComputer","Get-ADGroup","Get-ADOrganizationalUnit","Get-ADTrust","Get-ADDomain","Get-ADDomainController","DirectorySearcher","nltest")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnet1?\s+(group|user|accounts)\b"
| summarize Count=count(), Cmds=make_set(ProcessCommandLine,10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Devices=make_set(DeviceName) by AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where Count >= 3   // 3+ distinct AD-discovery invocations in 5 min = bulk enumeration, not a one-off admin lookup
| order by FirstSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Get-ADUser","Get-ADComputer","Get-ADGroup","Get-ADOrganizationalUnit","Get-ADTrust","Get-ADDomain","Get-ADDomainController","DirectorySearcher","nltest")
    or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnet1?\s+(group|user|accounts)\b"
| summarize Count=count(), Cmds=make_set(CommandLine,10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by Computer, SubjectUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Count >= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: PowerShell/net.exe Active Directory Enumeration Cmdlets
id: 6f2b1a54-9c3d-4e21-b7a0-3d8f1c22ab90
description: Detects AD discovery cmdlets/commands consistent with the vibe-coded AD mapping script reported by Huntress
references:
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/attacker-uses-suspected-ai-generated.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/17
tags:
  - attack.t1087.002
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1482
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\net1.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Get-ADUser'
      - 'Get-ADComputer'
      - 'Get-ADGroup'
      - 'Get-ADOrganizationalUnit'
      - 'Get-ADTrust'
      - 'Get-ADDomainController'
      - 'DirectorySearcher'
      - 'nltest'
      - 'net group'
      - 'net user'
  condition: selection_img and selection_cmd
level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\net.exe OR *\\net1.exe)) (@CommandLine:(*Get-ADUser* OR *Get-ADComputer* OR *Get-ADGroup* OR *Get-ADTrust* OR *Get-ADDomainController* OR *DirectorySearcher* OR *nltest* OR *"net group"* OR *"net user"*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|net1?)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/(Get-AD(User|Computer|Group|OrganizationalUnit|Trust|DomainController)|DirectorySearcher|nltest|net\s+(group|user|accounts))/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count(as=hits))
| hits >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe OR Processes.process_name=net.exe OR Processes.process_name=net1.exe) (Processes.process="*Get-ADUser*" OR Processes.process="*Get-ADComputer*" OR Processes.process="*Get-ADGroup*" OR Processes.process="*Get-ADOrganizationalUnit*" OR Processes.process="*Get-ADTrust*" OR Processes.process="*Get-ADDomainController*" OR Processes.process="*DirectorySearcher*" OR Processes.process="*nltest*" OR Processes.process="*net group*" OR Processes.process="*net user*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count>=3 | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe OR Processes.process_name=net.exe OR Processes.process_name=net1.exe) (Processes.process="*Get-ADUser*" OR Processes.process="*Get-ADComputer*" OR Processes.process="*Get-ADGroup*" OR Processes.process="*Get-ADOrganizationalUnit*" OR Processes.process="*Get-ADTrust*" OR Processes.process="*Get-ADDomainController*" OR Processes.process="*DirectorySearcher*" OR Processes.process="*nltest*" OR Processes.process="*net group*" OR Processes.process="*net user*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count>=3 | sort - lastTime
AD Inventory report artifact written (AD_Report.html + staged CSV/zip) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts when a PowerShell process writes 'AD_Report.html' — the exact filename the vibe-coded script produced to summarize its enumeration, alongside CSV exports it staged before archiving. This is a near-unique on-disk fingerprint of the campaign. Rationale: AD_Report.html is a verbatim, high-entropy filename named by Huntress as the script's final summary artifact — a near-unique disk IOC, so this warrants alerting tier with a low FP rate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/vibe-coded-malware-ai-powershell/
ATT&CKT1087.002 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal AD documentation/reporting tool that coincidentally names its output AD_Report.html
  • A blue-team detection-engineering test replaying the Huntress sample in a lab
  • A consultant's AD health-check deliverable saved with the same name
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Users\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-AD","DirectorySearcher","nltest")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the FolderPath and InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm whether the parent PowerShell also invoked Get-AD*/DirectorySearcher and whether sibling CSVs/a .zip were staged in the same directory. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the writing account, and preserve the staging folder for IR. 3) Hunt: search the host/user for s5cmd.exe and SharpShares.exe execution and for outbound archive uploads within the following hour.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "AD_Report.html"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "AD_Report.html"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="AD_Report.html" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
SharpShares network share enumeration execution AIReconnaissance High
Detects execution of SharpShares (a C# share-enumeration utility) the actor deployed ~30 minutes after AD mapping to hunt user-accessible data repositories while filtering out default admin shares. Matches on the binary name/version-info and the SharpShares command token even if renamed. Rationale: SharpShares is named explicitly by the article/Huntress as a deployed tool; matching the binary name, PE OriginalFileName (survives on-disk rename), and the SharpShares command token gives high fidelity at low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vibe-coded-powershell-script-active-directory/
ATT&CKT1135 T1069.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team/pentest engagement running SharpShares with authorization
  • Detection-engineering lab replay of the tool
  • Security researcher analyzing the sample on a managed host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cobaltstrike.exe") and FolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm no active authorized red-team ticket covers this host; review CommandLine for target scope and the parent process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the executing account, and capture the binary hash for scoping across the fleet. 3) Hunt: correlate with prior AD_Report.html/Get-AD* activity on the same session and look for s5cmd.exe exfil that typically follows share discovery.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "SharpShares.exe"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "SharpShares.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "SharpShares"

| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

s5cmd bulk file tool execution (S3-compatible exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects execution of s5cmd.exe — the legitimate high-speed S3 tool the actor staged in C:\ProgramData and abused to exfiltrate the archived AD inventory. Flags s5cmd invoked with transfer verbs (cp/sync/mv) or a custom --endpoint-url, especially when run from C:\ProgramData. Rationale: s5cmd.exe (staged at C:\ProgramData\s5cmd.exe per Huntress) is a rare binary in enterprise endpoints; pairing the name/OriginalFileName with transfer verbs or --endpoint-url isolates active exfiltration from benign presence. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://www.itsecurityguru.org/2026/07/08/huntress-uncovers-vibe-coded-malware-used-to-map-active-directory-environments/

1) Triage: extract the destination from --endpoint-url/bucket in CommandLine and confirm it is not a sanctioned corporate S3 endpoint; check the source folder for the AD inventory .zip. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress, isolate the host, disable the account and rotate any AWS/S3 credentials referenced. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents for the s5cmd process's outbound connections and volume, and scope other hosts running s5cmd.exe from C:\ProgramData.

RDP interactive logon followed by tool execution staged in C:\ProgramData AIDelivery Medium
Correlates a RemoteInteractive (RDP) logon by a non-machine account with execution of binaries staged in C:\ProgramData (or PowerShell referencing that path) within 2 hours — the exact initial-access-plus-staging pattern Huntress described (pre-compromised creds over RDP, tools dropped in ProgramData). Rationale: Directly encodes the article's initial-access chain (RDP with pre-compromised creds → tools staged/run from C:\ProgramData). The RDP-to-ProgramData-execution join suppresses benign ProgramData installers that aren't tied to a fresh remote session. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://securityaffairs.com/195321/hacking/attacker-used-ai-to-build-custom-powershell-recon-malware.html
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1078 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin RDPs to a server then runs a vendor installer/updater that lives in C:\ProgramData
  • Patch/agent deployment (e.g., EDR, monitoring agent) executing from ProgramData over an RDP admin session
  • Jump-host workflow where PowerShell scripts reference a ProgramData tools folder
  • MSP technician remoting in to run maintenance scripts
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("setup.exe","msiexec.exe","update.exe") and RemoteIP !startswith "10."
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the RemoteIP/geo and whether the account normally RDPs to this server; inspect the executed binaries in ProgramData (hash, signer) and their command lines. 2) Contain: if the logon source or binary is unrecognized, disable the account, terminate the RDP session, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: on confirmation pivot to Get-AD*/AD_Report.html, SharpShares.exe and s5cmd.exe on the same host, and review other RDP logons from the same source IP across the estate.
let Window = 2h;
let RdpLogons = DeviceLogonEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType == "LogonSuccess" and LogonType == "RemoteInteractive"
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project LogonTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteIP;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData\" and FileName endswith ".exe")
     or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has @"C:\ProgramData")
| join kind=inner RdpLogons on DeviceId, AccountName
| where Timestamp between (LogonTime .. LogonTime + Window)
| project LogonTime, ExecTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteIP, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by ExecTime desc
let Window = 2h;
let Rdp = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4624 and LogonType == 10
    | where not(TargetUserName endswith "$")
    | project LogonTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, TargetUserName, IpAddress;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName startswith @"C:\ProgramData\" and NewProcessName endswith ".exe")
     or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has @"C:\ProgramData")
| join kind=inner Rdp on Computer, $left.SubjectUserName == $right.TargetUserName
| where TimeGenerated between (LogonTime .. LogonTime + Window)
| project LogonTime, ExecTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, IpAddress, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by ExecTime desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@Image:(C\:\\ProgramData\\*.exe OR c\:\\programdata\\*.exe) OR (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:*ProgramData*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/\\ProgramData\\[^\\]+\.exe$/i OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/ProgramData/i))
| join({#event_simpleName=UserLogon LogonType=10}, field=aid, include=[UserName, RemoteAddressIP4])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName], function=count())

Suspected AI-generated AD enumeration script content in PowerShell logs AIInstallation High
Hunts PowerShell ScriptBlock (EID 4104) / AMSI content bearing the vibe-coded script's tell-tale strings — the prompt-iteration title '100% Working AD Information Gathering Script - FULLY FIXED' and its DC-discovery/report logic. Targets the script body itself rather than process metadata, catching it even if launched indirectly. Rationale: The prompt-iteration title '100% Working AD Information Gathering Script - FULLY FIXED' is a verbatim, high-entropy artifact of the LLM back-and-forth reported by Huntress — an almost signature-grade string that only appears in the script body, so it must be hunted in ScriptBlock/AMSI content. Defender AH has no canonical ScriptBlock content table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; use the PowerShell Operational feed via Sentinel or CrowdStrike AMSI instead. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/vibe-coded-malware-ai-powershell/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027 T1087.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst/IR replaying the published script string in a sandbox for detection testing
  • A blog/PoC copy of the script executed in a research VM
  • Threat-intel enrichment pipeline that echoes the string into a script comment
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "MALWARELAB" and Computer !has "IR-SANDBOX"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is not a sanctioned malware-analysis/detection-lab box; read the full ScriptBlockText to verify the DC-discovery cascade and export routine are present. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the executing account, and preserve the .ps1 and any C:\ProgramData staging folder. 3) Hunt: scope the same string across all endpoints, and correlate with AD_Report.html writes, SharpShares.exe and s5cmd.exe execution on the affected host.
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell" and EventID == 4104
| where RenderedDescription has_any ("100% Working AD Information Gathering Script","FULLY FIXED","AD Information Gathering Script")
    or (RenderedDescription has "AD_Report.html" and RenderedDescription has_any ("Get-ADDomainController","DirectorySearcher","nltest"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, RenderedDescription
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Misconfigured Server Reveals Three Evilginx Phishing Operations Targeting Microsoft 365

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 14 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An attacker running a live Microsoft 365 phishing operation left a Python web server listening on a public port with directory listing switched on. The command that did it:&nbsp;python3 -m http.server 8080, was still sitting in the readable&nbsp;.bash_history. From that one lapse, French security firm&nbsp;Lexfo&nbsp;lifted the operator's entire toolkit and pivoted through it to two more

M365 AiTM sign-in from Evilginx phishing infrastructure IPs (codemado / mail-argenta) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins whose source IP is one of the four Evilginx/SimpleHelp hosts Lexfo pulled from the misconfigured Budapest server. In an AiTM proxy the victim's live login is relayed through the operator's server, so the Microsoft-side sign-in shows the proxy IP, not the victim's — a direct, high-fidelity IOC pivot. Rationale: Uses the four second-source-corroborated infra IPs (185.163.204.7 hosted both the Evilginx proxy and SimpleHelp console) as direct sign-in-source IOCs; AiTM relays the real login so the Microsoft sign-in carries the proxy IP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1557 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher or IR team logging into a honeypot/decoy tenant from the same VPS range
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling that authenticates test accounts through a proxy
  • Shared-hosting IP reassignment months later to a benign SaaS the org legitimately uses
  • A pentest engagement deliberately routing M365 auth through a rented Budapest VPS
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the AccountUpn actually authenticated and pull the full sign-in row — ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, resource. Cross-check whether the same user signed in from a normal IP minutes before/after (AiTM proxy relay). Step 2 (contain): revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-registration of MFA. Block the four IPs at Conditional Access / firewall. Step 3 (hunt): search all sign-ins from these IPs across every account, then hunt for post-compromise mailbox rules, OAuth app consents, and token refreshes from unrelated geos on the affected accounts.

Microsoft 365 device-code-flow phishing sign-in (black-queen / saroula01) AIExploitation High
Hunts Entra ID sign-ins completed via the OAuth device code flow — the mechanism saroula01's black-queen fork abuses: a genuine device code wrapped in an Authenticator-themed lure, with the victim authorizing the attacker's session on real Microsoft infrastructure. Device code flow is rare in most orgs, so surfacing it (especially first-time-per-user and toward the Microsoft Authentication Broker app) is high-signal. Rationale: Device code flow is the exact mechanism the article says black-queen uses (real device code + genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin, so FIDO2/passkey origin binding does not help); Microsoft's Storm-2372 advisory confirms the same technique and the Microsoft Authentication Broker client-ID pivot for refresh-token/device-registration abuse. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://www.aha.org/h-isac-white-reports/2025-02-14-h-isac-tlp-white-threat-bulletin-storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code auth on genuinely input-constrained hardware (conference-room displays, IoT, some CLI tools like az login --use-device-code)
  • Developers using 'az login --use-device-code' or PowerShell Device Login on headless build agents
  • Smart-TV / Apple TV / streaming-stick enrollment of a corporate Teams Rooms account
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that still rely on device code grant
Suppression filter
| where not(Apps has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and array_length(IPs) == 1)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): for each surfaced UPN, check whether device code flow is expected for that user/device class; inspect the target app (flag Microsoft Authentication Broker / device registration service — per Storm-2372 that path leads to PRT theft) and the IP/geo of the completing sign-in. Step 2 (contain): revoke sessions and refresh tokens for the user, disable device code flow via a Conditional Access authentication-flow policy, and review/remove any attacker-registered devices in Entra ID. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the same IPs and app IDs across all accounts, review non-interactive refresh activity, and check for newly joined/registered devices and mailbox exfil rules on affected identities.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| extend ProcDetails = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where ProcDetails has "Device Code"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), Apps=make_set(Application,10), Countries=make_set(Country,10) by AccountUpn
| order by FirstSeen desc
SigninLogs

| extend ProcDetails = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where ProcDetails has "Device Code"
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,10), Apps=make_set(AppDisplayName,10), Countries=make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion),10) by UserPrincipalName
| order by FirstSeen desc

Stolen M365 session token refresh — same account, many IPs, non-interactive (token aging) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the article's described behaviour of operators refreshing stolen tokens as they age out — the same corporate mailbox captured repeatedly from different IPs, and black-queen's autoRefresh tokens re-refreshed up to 25 times. Detects a single account accruing an abnormal number of distinct source IPs on non-interactive (refresh-token) sign-ins in a short window. Rationale: Directly models the article's 'repeated captures of the same accounts from different IPs' and autoRefresh tokens refreshed up to 25 times; non-interactive + high distinct-IP fan-out per account isolates token replay from normal user roaming. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mobile users roaming across carrier/Wi-Fi networks generating many refresh IPs
  • Corporate VPN or SASE egress that rotates public IPs per session
  • Background Office/Outlook/Teams token refreshes across multiple devices for one power user
  • Shared service/kiosk account legitimately used from many locations
Suppression filter
| where not(Apps has_any ("Microsoft VPN Client","Microsoft Intune") )
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): review the IP/geo/ASN spread and app mix for the flagged account — legitimate roaming clusters by carrier/VPN ASN, whereas token theft shows unrelated hosting/VPS ASNs. Correlate against any interactive AiTM or device-code sign-in for the same user. Step 2 (contain): revoke all refresh tokens and sessions, reset credentials, and apply a short sign-in frequency + CAE-capable Conditional Access policy so a reset actually invalidates stolen tokens. Step 3 (hunt): enumerate mailbox rules, OAuth consents, and forwarding added during the window; check whether any of the fan-out IPs overlap the known Evilginx infra IPs and pivot to other victims.

| where IsInteractive == false
| summarize DistinctIPs=dcount(IPAddress), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), Countries=make_set(Country,20), Refreshes=count() by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1d)
| where DistinctIPs >= 5   // >=5 distinct refresh-token source IPs/day for one account = token-replay fan-out
| order by DistinctIPs desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs

| summarize DistinctIPs=dcount(IPAddress), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), Apps=make_set(AppDisplayName,20), Refreshes=count() by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| where DistinctIPs >= 5   // >=5 distinct refresh-token source IPs/day for one account = token-replay fan-out
| order by DistinctIPs desc

Endpoint connections to Evilginx phishing landing domains (picis.net / romnor.ca) AIDelivery High
Hunts managed endpoints resolving or connecting to the three phishing domains tied to the operations — picis[.]net and romnor[.]ca (plus queeenspropertyservices[.]ca) — which fronted the Evilginx AiTM proxies and their rotating wildcard subdomains. A hit means a user reached the phishing landing page and is a candidate victim before/at credential capture. Rationale: picis[.]net and romnor[.]ca are named as the two phishing domains and queeenspropertyservices[.]ca is in the IOC bundle; picis[.]net was still provisioning new subdomains as late as May 2026, so wildcard matching catches rotating hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst manually detonating the phishing URL from a corporate host during triage
  • Threat-intel sandbox/crawler VM resolving the domains for enrichment
  • URL-reputation or email-security appliance pre-fetching links from a managed endpoint
  • Domain later parked/reassigned to a benign owner after takedown, generating benign lookups
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the user and process that made the request (browser vs automated tool) and whether a sign-in followed on the same identity shortly after (candidate AiTM capture). Step 2 (contain): sinkhole/block the three domains and their wildcards at DNS/proxy, and if the user authenticated, revoke sessions + reset credentials + re-register MFA. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the resolved IPs (cross-check the four Evilginx infra IPs), search email/Safe Links telemetry for the delivering message and other recipients, and check for subsequent device-code or token-refresh anomalies on the affected account.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("picis.net","romnor.ca","queeenspropertyservices.ca")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("picis.net","romnor.ca","queeenspropertyservices.ca")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

SecurityEvent

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

let BadHashes = dynamic(["6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018"]);

jscrambler npm package publishes malicious preinstall binary

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 13 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 11, 2026, version 8.14.0 of jscrambler was published to npm carrying a malicious preinstall hook that drops and executes a platform-specific native binary on Linux, Windows, and macOS. jscrambler is the official CLI client for the Jscrambler Code Integrity API, a commercial JavaScript obfuscation and web-app protection service, with a clean version history dating back to 0.1.0. The compromised release was flagged by StepSecurity's AI Release Analyzer with a suspicion score of 0 (the maximum suspicion rating) on publish.

Malicious jscrambler npm package (8.14.0+) drops native binary container dist/intro.js AIDelivery High
Hunts creation of the 7.8 MB dist/intro.js custom binary container inside node_modules/jscrambler on install of the compromised 8.14.0/8.16.0-8.20.0 releases. Legitimate jscrambler ships intro.js only as small JavaScript, so a multi-MB intro.js under that package path is the supply-chain artifact. Rationale: Anchors on the exact article artifact: node_modules/jscrambler/dist/intro.js at ~7.8 MB (vs KB-sized legit JS). Path + size cleanly separates the compromised 8.14.0/8.16.0-8.20.0 releases from clean 8.13.0. Corroborated by Socket.dev and cirosec IOC list. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://cirosec.de/en/news/iocs_cryto_stealer_supply_chain_incident/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately vendoring a large asset named intro.js into an unrelated node_modules path (rare; size+jscrambler path filter suppresses)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox for analysis
  • Backup/restore or npm cache repopulation replaying the same malicious tarball on a re-image
  • Internal mirror that cached 8.14.0 before it was pulled, re-serving it to CI runners
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node") and FileSize between (5000000 .. 20000000)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually installed the compromised release - grep package-lock.json/node_modules/jscrambler/package.json for version 8.14.0/8.16.0/8.17.0/8.18.0/8.20.0 and check for the 5-byte magic header 1B 43 53 49 01 in intro.js. 2) Contain: isolate the host/CI runner, kill any detached temp-dir process, and pin/rebuild with jscrambler 8.13.0. 3) Hunt: rotate every credential exposed to that host (cloud/AWS/Azure/GCP keys, CI tokens, browser sessions, Bitwarden vault, crypto wallet seed phrases) and search the fleet for the same intro.js artifact and outbound calls to the C2 IPs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has "jscrambler" and FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where FileName =~ "intro.js"
| where FileSize > 5000000   // legit intro.js is a few KB; 7.8 MB = binary container
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has "jscrambler" and TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| where TargetFileName =~ "intro.js"
| where TargetFileSize > 5000000   // 7.8 MB container vs KB-sized legit JS
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Execution of jscrambler IronWorm stealer payload by known SHA256 AIInstallation High
Alerts on process execution matching the three extracted native payload hashes (ELF/PE32+/Mach-O) dropped from dist/intro.js. This is the highest-fidelity pivot: a direct hash match on the cross-platform IronWorm stealer binary regardless of its randomized temp-dir filename. Rationale: Direct match on the three extracted payload SHA256s (ELF/PE32+/Mach-O) named in the article IOC table - randomized temp filenames make hash the only stable execution pivot. Confirmed by The Hacker News and cirosec. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://cirosec.de/en/news/iocs_cryto_stealer_supply_chain_incident/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in an EDR-monitored sandbox
  • Purple-team/atomic-red-team style validation of this exact detection
  • AV/EDR quarantine copy being scanned (usually a scan action, not a process create) - verify ActionType is process creation not a scan
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a hash match on live malware - treat as confirmed. Capture the process tree (parent should be node.exe/npm running the preinstall) and the temp-dir image path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and preserve the temp binary for forensics. 3) Hunt: on any host with a hit, immediately rotate all reachable credentials (cloud keys, CI tokens, browser sessions, Bitwarden vault, wallet seed phrases) and pivot to network egress toward 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 to scope C2 activity.

| where SHA256 in ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/node preinstall spawns detached hidden binary from OS temp directory AIInstallation Medium
Behavioral, variant-resilient detection for the loader: dist/setup.js decompresses a platform binary to a randomly named dotfile in the OS temp dir and spawns it detached from the install tree. Catches the 8.16.0-8.20.0 re-releases and any repack that changes the payload hash. Rationale: Encodes the article's loader mechanics exactly - parent node/npm, child is a random dotfile (`.[a-z0-9]{6,}(.exe)`) in the OS temp dir, spawned detached. Hash-independent so it survives the 8.16.0-8.20.0 repacks confirmed by Socket.dev. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://cirosec.de/en/news/iocs_cryto_stealer_supply_chain_incident/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / prebuild-install extracting a legitimate signed native addon to temp during install
  • Electron or Playwright/puppeteer postinstall unpacking browser binaries into a temp cache
  • esbuild/swc/other native-toolchain packages caching a platform binary in temp
  • CI runners with ephemeral temp dirs where any tool writes dotfiles - baseline per pipeline
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install","playwright","puppeteer","electron") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child binary's SHA256 and folder path; check whether the parent npm command referenced jscrambler and whether the image is signed. Unsigned random dotfile from node = high suspicion. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner and kill the detached process (it is unref'd from npm, so it survives install exit). 3) Hunt: submit the hash to intel, then sweep for the three known payload hashes and outbound connections to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 across the fleet; rotate credentials on confirmed hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/")
| where FileName startswith "."   // randomly named dotfile dropped by the loader
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","node")
| where ActingProcessName startswith "." or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\.", @"\Local\Temp\.", "/tmp/.", "/var/folders/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: node/npm Spawns Hidden Binary From OS Temp Directory
id: c9f2a7d1-3e64-4b18-8a92-5d0c1f7e2b34
description: Detects node.exe/npm spawning a randomly named dotfile executable from the OS temp directory, matching the jscrambler preinstall loader behaviour.

detection:

  condition: selection
falsepositives:

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^node(\.exe)?$|^npm(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/(\\Temp\\|\/tmp\/|\/var\/folders\/.*\/)\.[a-z0-9]{6,}(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","node","npm.exe") (Processes.process_path="*\\Temp\\.*" OR Processes.process_path="*/tmp/.*" OR Processes.process_path="*/var/folders/*/.*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
jscrambler stealer C2 egress to hardcoded IPs and Tor endpoints AICommand & Control High
Alerts on outbound connections to the two hardcoded C2 IPs (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) and the Tor bootstrap domains (check/archive.torproject.org) the dropped IronWorm binary uses to exfiltrate stolen credentials. High-fidelity on the IPs; Tor domains add context. Rationale: The two IPs are hardcoded C2 confirmed by Harden-Runner monitoring plus cirosec/ThreatFox second sources; combined with the Tor bootstrap domains the stealer uses for exfil. IP match is near-zero FP; Tor domains give the analyst egress context. Cross-checked against: • https://cirosec.de/en/news/iocs_cryto_stealer_supply_chain_incident/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Tor Browser users on the host hitting check.torproject.org (only the *.torproject.org clause, never the two IPs)
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively probing the C2 IPs
  • Security scanner/EDR sandbox validating connectivity to the IOCs
  • Shared NAT egress where another host's Tor traffic is attributed - confirm the initiating process
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process - a hit where the process is a temp-dir dotfile or node child is a confirmed stealer beacon; a browser hitting only the Tor domain is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host and block 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: on confirmed beacons, rotate every credential the host could reach (cloud/AWS/Azure/GCP, CI tokens, browser sessions, Bitwarden, wallet seeds) and sweep the fleet for the intro.js artifact, the three payload hashes, and any other host contacting these IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
    or RemoteUrl in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
    or DstHostname in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
